title: Guides for prayer (CCC 2685–2690)
hook: families, clergy, religious, prayer groups, spiritual directors

segments.voice: Yesterday, the way of prayer: to the Father, through Jesus, in the Spirit. Your line was to, through, in. Did you try the three short words, Come, Holy Spirit, before something that mattered? Day one thousand one hundred forty-four.

Jesus has just finished praying, somewhere off to the side, and his disciples have been watching. They've been with him a while now. They've seen the healings, heard the parables. And when he comes back, the thing one of them asks for isn't a miracle or an explanation. It's a lesson. In the Douay-Rheims: "Lord, teach us to pray, as John also taught his disciples." The ones closest to him, who have seen all of it, still ask to be taught. Today the Catechism asks who does that teaching now. Today: guides for prayer.
screen: `HE FINISHES PRAYING.` → `LORD, TEACH US TO PRAY.` → `WHO TEACHES NOW?`

segments.voice: The Catechism's answer begins at home. It calls the Christian family the first place where prayer is learned, and it gives that home a name: the domestic church. A grace before supper, a sign of the cross on a sleeping child's forehead, a parent kneeling by a bed. In the Catechism's picture, that's where a child first sees what praying looks like. Paul points to the same thing when he writes to Timothy about a faith that lived first in his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice, before it lived in him. Then the Church's ministers. Priests and deacons, the Catechism says, are responsible for forming people in prayer, not only for leading it. Next, people in religious life, monks, nuns, sisters and brothers, many of whom have given their lives to prayer. Their monasteries and convents keep a rhythm that others can join or learn from. Then prayer groups, which the Catechism calls schools of prayer: a few people around a table, a Bible open, a rosary passed around a parish hall. And last, spiritual direction. Some Catholics meet regularly with one wise person, a priest, a sister or a trained lay guide, to talk honestly about their prayer. The Catechism, drawing on John of the Cross, says that choice matters: a guide should be learned, prudent and experienced. In this picture, nobody is expected to work prayer out alone in a locked room. Even the disciples, standing next to Jesus, asked.
screen: `THE FAMILY: A DOMESTIC CHURCH.` · `MINISTERS AND RELIGIOUS.` · `PRAYER GROUPS: SCHOOLS OF PRAYER.` · `A SPIRITUAL DIRECTOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think of who taught you. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person who showed you how to pray, or how to be still, or how to hope. A grandparent, a teacher, a friend, a stranger in a pew. See their face. Then think of one person you could ask to teach you a little more. If you pray, you can thank God for the first and ask for courage with the second. If you don't, simply hold both of them in mind. The bell holds the time.
Guides for prayer. In the Catechism: families, ordained ministers, religious, prayer groups and spiritual directors, the people who teach others to pray. Today's words.
Your line: nobody learns alone. Today, ask someone one real question about how they pray, or how they keep going, and listen to the whole answer. Day one thousand one hundred forty-four.

howItsDone: Catholics usually first learn prayer at home, then through parish catechesis, prayer groups and retreats; some meet regularly with a spiritual director to talk about their prayer life.
